title: Tries and union-find
description: Prefix trees for word lookups and autocomplete, and union-find for merging groups and spotting cycles.

challenges.title: Implement a Trie (Operations List)
challenges.prompt:
A **trie** (prefix tree) stores words one letter per level, so words that begin the same way share a path from the root. Build one and replay a list of operations on it:

- `["insert", word]` adds `word`.
- `["search", word]` is `true` only if `word` itself was inserted earlier.
- `["startsWith", prefix]` is `true` if at least one inserted word begins with `prefix`.

Return a list with the result of every `search` and `startsWith`, in order; `insert` produces no output. Each operation should take O(L) time for a word of length L, however many words are stored.

examples.explain: "car" is only a prefix until it is inserted as a word of its own.

constraints: Words contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Each node needs two things: a map from letter to child node, and a flag that says "a word ends here".

insert walks letter by letter, creating missing children, then sets the end flag on the last node. search and startsWith share one helper that walks the letters and returns the node it stops on, or nothing if a letter is missing.
search needs the walk to succeed and the end flag to be set; startsWith only needs the walk to succeed.
challenges.explanation: Every node maps letters to children and carries an end-of-word flag. Inserting walks the word, creating missing nodes, and marks the last one. search and startsWith both walk the same path; the only difference is that search also requires the end flag, which is why "car" is not found after inserting only "card". Each operation touches one node per letter, so it costs O(L) no matter how many words are stored.

complexity.time: O(L) per operation for a word of length L

challenges.title: Autocomplete Suggestions
challenges.prompt:
You are building the suggestion list under a search box. Given a list of distinct lowercase `words` and the text `typed`, which the user enters one letter at a time, return a list with one entry per letter typed.

Entry `i` holds the words that start with the first `i + 1` letters of `typed`: at most three of them, the three that come first in alphabetical order, listed in that order. If no word starts with that prefix, the entry is an empty list.

examples.explain: After "c", "ca" and "car" the three alphabetically smallest matches are car, care and cargo. Only cart starts with "cart".
No word starts with "apz", so the last entry is empty.

constraints: All strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Filtering and sorting every word for every prefix works but repeats a lot of effort. All of the matches for a prefix live below one trie node.
Insert the words in sorted order. As a word passes through a node, append it to that node's suggestion list if the list has fewer than three entries.
Then walk `typed` letter by letter: each node you reach already holds its answer. Once a letter is missing, every later entry is empty.
challenges.explanation: Every word that starts with a prefix sits in the subtree under that prefix's trie node. Inserting the words in alphabetical order lets each node keep its own top three as words pass through it, so answering the query is just a walk down `typed`, one node per letter. Sorting costs O(n log n) comparisons, building costs O(total letters), and each answer is read in O(1). A sort plus binary search for each prefix is a good alternative worth mentioning.

complexity.time: O(n log n + S + T) for n words with S letters in total and T typed letters

challenges.title: Word Dictionary With Wildcards
challenges.pattern: Trie with depth-first search for wildcards
challenges.prompt:
Build a word dictionary that supports wildcard search, then replay `ops` on it:

- `["add", word]` stores a lowercase word.
- `["search", pattern]` is `true` if some stored word has the same length as `pattern` and matches it letter by letter, where a `.` in the pattern matches any single letter.

Return the results of the `search` operations in order.

examples.explain: "ca" is too short to match any stored word, and no three-letter word starts with d and ends with t.

constraints: Patterns contain lowercase letters and dots
hints: Store the words in a trie. A pattern without dots is an ordinary trie search.
A dot means "any child". Write a recursive match(node, i) that handles letter i of the pattern starting from node.
For a dot, try every child and return true as soon as one branch matches. At the end of the pattern, the answer is the node's end-of-word flag.
challenges.explanation: Adding is a normal trie insert. Searching walks the pattern: a letter follows one child, a dot branches into every child, and reaching the end of the pattern succeeds only on a node that ends a word, which also enforces the exact length. Without dots a search costs O(L). Each dot can multiply the branches by up to 26, so the worst case is O(26^d * L) for d dots, but the trie prunes every branch that no stored word follows.

complexity.time: O(L) to add; O(L) to search without dots, up to O(26^d * L) with d dots

challenges.title: Find All Words in a Letter Grid
challenges.prompt:
Given a grid of lowercase letters `board` and a list of distinct `words`, return every word that can be traced in the grid. You trace a word by starting on any cell and stepping to a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell for each next letter. A cell can be used at most once within the same word.

Return the found words in any order. Searching the grid separately for every word is too slow when the list is long: search for all of them in one pass.

examples.explain: "seat" uses (0,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,0). "near" and "dense" cannot be traced: no a sits next to an e that touches the n, and no e touches the d.
b and c are diagonal, so "abcd" cannot be traced, and "dd" would reuse the only d.

constraints: All letters are lowercase English letters
hints: Running the single-word search once per word repeats the same grid walks for words that share a prefix. Put all the words in a trie instead.
Start a depth-first search from every cell and carry the current trie node. Step into a neighbor only if the trie has a child for its letter, so dead prefixes stop immediately.
When you reach a node that ends a word, record the word and clear the mark so it is reported once. Mark cells as used while they are on the current path and restore them on the way back.
challenges.explanation: All words go into one trie, so a single depth-first search from each cell explores every word at once and abandons a path as soon as its letters stop being a prefix of any word. Cells on the current path are overwritten with # and restored afterward, the usual backtracking move. Removing a word's mark after finding it avoids duplicates, and deleting empty trie branches stops later searches from walking into finished areas.

complexity.time: O(R * C * 4 * 3^(L - 1)) in the worst case for words up to length L

challenges.title: Redundant Connection
challenges.prompt:
A network of `n` computers labeled `1` to `n` was cabled as a tree: every computer reachable from every other, with no loops. Then one extra cable was added between two computers that were not already directly connected.

You get all `n` cables as `edges`, a list of pairs `[a, b]`. Return the cable whose removal turns the network back into a tree. If more than one cable would work, return the one that appears last in `edges`.

examples.explain: Removing any of the three cables leaves a tree; [2, 3] comes last.
The loop is 2-3-5-4-2. Of its cables, [5, 3] appears last.

constraints: 1 <= a, b <= n and a != b
hints: Add the cables one at a time. The first cable whose two ends are already connected is the one that closes the loop.
Union-find answers "are a and b already connected?" in nearly O(1): compare find(a) and find(b), and union them if they differ.

Why is the first failing union the right answer even with the "appears last" rule? The only cables you could remove are the ones on the loop, and the loop is not complete until its last cable arrives.
challenges.explanation: Union-find with path halving and union by rank processes the cables in order. A union that finds both ends already in the same set means this cable closes a cycle. Exactly one cycle exists, the removable cables are exactly the cycle's cables, and the cycle only closes when the last of them arrives, so the first failed union is the cable that appears last among them.

challenges.title: Is It a Valid Tree?
challenges.prompt: You have `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n - 1` and a list of undirected `edges`. Return `true` if the edges join the nodes into one valid tree: every node can reach every other node, and there are no cycles. No edge is repeated and no edge joins a node to itself.

examples.explain: Three edges for four nodes is the right count, but they form a cycle and node 3 is cut off.

hints: A tree on n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges. That check alone is not enough (see the third example), but it rules out a lot.
With union-find, a union whose two ends already share a root means the edge closes a cycle.
If there are exactly n - 1 edges and none of them closes a cycle, every union merged two groups, so n groups became 1: the graph is connected.
challenges.explanation: A tree needs exactly n - 1 edges, so any other count fails immediately. With that count, each union either merges two groups or reveals a cycle. If all n - 1 unions succeed, the number of groups dropped from n to 1, so the graph is connected and acyclic. A DFS that checks for revisits and counts reached nodes is an equally good answer.

challenges.title: Satisfiable Equality Equations
challenges.prompt: Each string in `equations` has four characters and looks like `"a==b"` or `"a!=b"`, where the letters are single lowercase variable names (the two letters may be the same). Return `true` if you can give every variable an integer so that all of the equations hold at once.

examples.explain: p equals q and q equals r, so p must equal r.
For example a = b = 1 and c = d = 2.

constraints: Every equation is 4 characters: letter, "==" or "!=", letter
hints: Equalities chain together: every variable linked by == ends up in one group that must share a value.
Make one pass that unions the two sides of every "==" equation, using 26 slots for the letters.

Then make a second pass over the "!=" equations. If both sides have the same root, the equations contradict each other. Order matters: checking a != before all the == are merged can miss a contradiction.
challenges.explanation: Equality is transitive, so the == equations split the letters into groups that must share a value, which is exactly what union-find builds. Once every group is final, an != equation is impossible only when both sides landed in the same group. Any assignment that gives each group its own number satisfies the rest. With only 26 letters the sets stay tiny, so plain parent links are enough here.

complexity.time: O(E) for E equations (26 letters keep each find short)
